before: as const asks the checker to retain literal values and readonly properties for this literal expression. For [2, 4], it produces a readonly two-position tuple rather than a general mutable number array. A tuple describes fixed positions with separately known types; here those positions retain the literal types 2 and 4. For {kind:"home"}, kind keeps the literal type "home" and is readonly through this typed value.

The checker rejects position[0] = 9 through this readonly tuple. Ordinary const only protects the binding; as const additionally changes the inferred type of the literal. A precise explicitly written readonly type can express an equivalent contract.
Create originPoint as a readonly two-position tuple with values 0 and 0, retaining each literal type 0. An as const assertion or an equivalent explicit readonly tuple type is accepted.
after: A tuple is an array type with known positions. `as const` keeps exact literal types and makes this array literal a readonly tuple. Readonly means these positions cannot be assigned new values through this type.

Assigning to position[0] is rejected, even if you try to assign 2 again. Plain const only stops replacing the variable's value; as const adds readonly type information. It does not freeze the object while JavaScript runs.
Create originPoint as a readonly pair containing 0 and 0, keeping each exact literal type. You may use as const or an equivalent written readonly tuple type.
